newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures came under pressure from a second wave of selling by non-residents on Tuesday but recovered with Bunds, partly on the back of domestic demand for bonds.

Traders said the decision by Prime Minister Alain Juppe to resign whatever the outcome of the second round of voting on June 1 was seen as positive for the centre-right and some were expecting the ruling coalition to scrape home.
This more positive view prompted many to cover short positions, pushing June PIBOR up nine basis points to 96.30. The spread over Euromarks, however, was still above 50 basis points.
The main focus was on the likely replacement for Juppe and outgoing National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin was seen as one of the frontrunners.

A PIBOR trader also said despite his previous anti-Maastricht declarations, Seguin's republican views meant he could attract more voters for the right and that he would probably toe the pro-monetary union line once in power.
He said traders were not keen to sell as PIBOR would look expensive compared with Euromarks in the event of a centre-right victory and a win for the left would not produce a dramatic selloff anyway.
He said the worst possible outcome was actually a hung parliament with either the Communists or National Front, both hardened anti-EMU parties, holding the balance of power in the National Assembly.

A bond futures trader said the late rally in the June bond future, which hauled the contract back to its opening level at 128.46, was partly sparked by talk of a U.S. house buying 10-year Bunds and selling 10-year U.S. notes.
He said it drove Bunds through key technical resistance levels and in turn hoisted the French future higher. The French contract had earlier survived a test of 128.10/12 support.

The 10-year yield spread between French and German bonds dipped to minus eight early in the session before returning to trade unchanged at minus 10 basis points on the back of demand for bonds from domestic investors.
Dominique Barbet, bond analyst at Banques Paribas, said domestic investors appeared unconcerned whether the left come to power or the centre-right coalition retained its majority.

"There's a high probability we will have a left government, but the conclusion investors draw is that whether it's the left of the right it won't put France's economic policies in question," Barbet said.
He said investors expected France to continue its current policy of trimming public deficits and to remain committed to the timetable for a single European currency.
Analysts said one factor behind the buying was that domestic investors were preparing for a flood of cash from bond redemptions by turning cash into bonds whenever yields rose.

The French franc strengthened against the mark amid renewed weakness for the German unit against the dollar. It climbed as high as 3.3732 per mark from a low of 3.3777. The franc was at 3.3714 prior to the release of the first election results.
